newsitem.title: UK: Russian businessmen sue Forbes Magazine for libel.
newsitem.headline: Russian businessmen sue Forbes Magazine for libel.

text.p: Two leading Russian businessman on Wednesday sued Forbes magazine for libel over an article their lawyer said was "defamatory and inflammatory."

The libel writs were issued in the London High Court by entrepreneur Boris Berezovsky, who is now Deputy Secretary of Russia's National Security Council, and Nikolai Glushkov, First Deputy Managing Director of the Russian airline Aeroflot.
Their lawyers are seeking a retraction in court by the international business magazine. If the libel case goes to trial, they would expect a jury to decide on damages of at least 100,000 pounds.
Lawyer Ed Mishkin said the article in the December 30 edition of the U.S.-based magazine was "highly defamatory, inflammatory and false."

Asked why the two had chosen to go to court in London, Mishkin told a news conference: "Both men have considerable contacts in this country, their reputation is very important to them in this country and Forbes is widely distributed in this country."
The writ claimed that Berezovsky was defamed in connection with the 1995 Moscow killing of Russian television network head Vladislav Listiev.

Berezovsky, quoted by his lawyers in a statement, said: "Vladislav Listiev was my colleague and friend. To suggest that I had anything to do with his tragic death is a hurtful, shameful lie that must be retracted."

"I come from a country that, unfortunately, knows something about a big lie and I am stunned that a magazine with the international reputation of Forbes would resort to a lie to meet with me and then use a series of lies to defame me."
Glushkov sued the magazine over allegations that he had a criminal record.

The Aeroflot executive, again quoted by the lawyers, said "This accusation is totally false and would be considered comical if it were not so damaging to my reputation ... I have not been charged with any crime in my entire life."
Berezovsky has courted controversy at almost every turn in his meteoric rise from car dealer to Kremlin politician and his current role negotiating in Chechnya was no exception.
Loathed by communists and many business rivals alike, the entrepreneur who made a fortune under market reforms epitomises all that many Russians despise.

But, dismissing critics' jibes that he is using politics for personal gain, Berezovsky says he is one of a new breed of businessmen-turned-politicians whose role is to spread the word of market reforms and guarantee that they continue.
